=== ATCH EXHIBIT A_Generalized Cost-Benefit Analysis of Data Center Conversion to Immersion Cooling.pdf ===
Issue: Water-based evaporative cooling in data centers imposes significant environmental and
financial burdens compared to immersion cooling with non-PFAS dielectric fluids.


Rule: Data center cooling must balance energy efficiency (PUE), water use, maintenance, insurance,
and regulatory compliance. Water cooling typically achieves a PUE of 1.5, consuming hundreds of
millions of gallons annually for evaporation, leading to ecosystem strain and health risks from
recycled water. Immersion cooling submerges servers in non-conductive fluids, achieving PUE ~1.1,
near-zero water use, reduced maintenance, and non-flammable benefits. Non-PFAS fluids cost
$30–60/gallon with low recycling fees ($10–25/gallon). TCO savings of 30–40% are typical for
immersion vs. water, with ROI in 2–5 years for conversions.


Argument: Water cooling's environmental impact is severe: a 100 MW facility consumes 730 million
gallons/year (2 million gallons/day) via evaporation, straining local resources. Recycling treated
water into ecosystems costs ~$1.5 million/year for mitigation (removing additives, preventing thermal
pollution), with residual risks to biodiversity ($500,000/year in offsets/fines). Community exposure to
recycled water with trace chemicals elevates health risks costing $1 million/year. Financially, water
cooling has low upfront CAPEX ($15 million new-build) but high 10-year TCO ($650 million), driven
by energy ($50 million/year at PUE 1.5, $0.10/kWh), maintenance ($2 million/year for
corrosion/mineral buildup), and water procurement ($3.65 million/year at $0.005/gallon). No
insurance discounts apply due to fire risks.


Immersion cooling eliminates these issues. For new construction, non-PFAS fluids yield TCO of
$390–440 million over 10 years (32–40% savings vs. water), with higher initial CAPEX ($18.9–21.3
million, including $1.8–4.2 million fluid fill at $30–60/gallon) offset by OPEX reductions: 40% lower
energy (PUE 1.1, $30 million/year), 70–80% less maintenance ($350,000–450,000/year due to
dielectric protection), and 15% insurance savings ($300,000/year for non-flammability). Zero water
use avoids $3 million/year externalities. Non-PFAS biodegradability/recyclability keeps disposal low
($10–25/gallon).


For conversions, upfront costs ($28–42 million for retrofits, servers, fill, and phased downtime) yield
TCO of $370–480 million (26–43% below water), with similar OPEX savings and ROI of 150–190%
for non-PFAS (payback 2–3.5 years). Energy savings alone ($20 million/year) drive payback in 2–4
years, while closed-loop longevity (12–15 years) defers replacements.


Conclusion: Water cooling is environmentally unsustainable and financially inferior due to high
water/energy/maintenance costs and externalities. Immersion cooling with non-PFAS fluids offers
 superior TCO (32–43% savings), rapid ROI (2–3.5 years for conversions), and zero water impact,
making it the clear choice for new builds and retrofits.


Sources:
Water consumption: ~730M gallons/year for 100 MW –
https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/data-centers-and-water-consumption

Externalities (~$3M/year):
https://ethicalgeo.org/the-cloud-is-drying-our-rivers-water-usage-of-ai-data-centers

TCO savings 30–40%:
https://www.datacenterfrontier.com/sponsored/article/55261111/meeting-data-center-cooling-demand

=== Comments on Proposal for Publication of 16 TAC §25.194 – Project No. 58481_signed.pdf ===
Subject: Comments on Proposal for Publication of 16 TAC §25.194 – Project No. 58481
Submitted by: Jason Buster
Date: 30 March 2026
Introduction
I appreciate the Commission's work to implement Senate Bill 6 through the Proposal for
Publication (PFP) of new 16 TAC §25.194. The proposed standards—including financial
commitments (e.g., deposits with high forfeiture for withdrawal), site control proof, end-use
customer disclosure, backup generation disclosure, study fees, operational milestones, and
refund mechanisms—directly advance the mandate in PURA §37.0561(b) to support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.
To further strengthen these goals, the final rule should explicitly consider operational resilience
factors that impact long-term project viability and reduce the risk of withdrawal after
interconnection commitments are made.

Core Argument: Water-Intensive Cooling Increases Stranded Cost Risks
Large loads, particularly data centers, often rely on evaporative cooling, which consumes
enormous water volumes (e.g., approximately 730 million gallons per year for a 100 MW facility,
or ~2 million gallons per day). In Texas’ water-scarce environment, this creates substantial risks,
including:
    ●​ Drought-induced supply restrictions or interruptions.
    ●​ Permitting delays, denials, or local opposition from groundwater districts or TCEQ.
    ●​ Operational curtailments, forced relocations, or early project abandonment if water
        access becomes unsustainable.

These scenarios can lead to project withdrawal post-interconnection, even after transmission
upgrades begin, resulting in stranded infrastructure costs socialized to ratepayers. While the
proposed forfeiture provisions (e.g., high percentages for late-stage withdrawal) mitigate some
harm, proactive screening of viability factors is more effective for preventing such outcomes and
aligning with PURA §37.0561 objectives.

Evidence: Immersion Cooling as a Lower-Risk, More Resilient Alternative
Attached as Exhibit A is a generalized cost-benefit analysis comparing traditional evaporative
cooling to immersion cooling using non-PFAS dielectric fluids. Key findings include:
    ●​ Immersion achieves PUE ~1.1 (vs. ~1.5 for evaporative), delivering ~40% energy
       savings.
    ●​ Near-zero direct water use eliminates drought and permitting vulnerabilities.
    ●​ 30–43% lower 10-year total cost of ownership (TCO) for conversions ($370–480 million
       vs. $650 million for evaporative), with rapid ROI (2–3.5 years) driven by energy,
       maintenance (70–80% reduction), insurance savings (15% for non-flammability), and
       avoided externalities ($3 million/year in water-related mitigation, health, and biodiversity
       costs).
    ●​ Superior long-term viability, making projects more likely to meet milestones, sustain
       operations, and avoid forfeiture/withdrawal events.




                                                                                                 1/3
 These attributes position immersion-cooled (or equivalent low/zero-water) designs as
economically and operationally superior, directly reducing stranded cost risks.

Primary Recommendations: Minor Expansions to the Proposed Rule
To better minimize stranded risks under PURA §37.0561(b):
    1.​ Require disclosure of primary cooling technology type (e.g., evaporative,
        immersion, closed-loop dry, etc.) as part of the interconnection application and site
        control materials, analogous to the proposed backup generation disclosure. This adds
        transparency without mandating specific technology and enables better assessment of
        long-term viability during studies.
    2.​ Provide consideration or preference in interconnection studies, milestone evaluations,
        or refund determinations for designs implementing non-PFAS immersion cooling. This
        could include weighted criteria or expedited elements for lower-risk projects, incentivizing
        sustainable developments aligned with reliability and cost minimization.

Secondary Recommendation: Interagency Coordination with TCEQ
While PUCT's authority centers on interconnection and reliability, water-related risks for large
loads intersect with TCEQ's jurisdiction over air/ water permits, discharges, and environmental
standards. The Commission could enhance the rule's effectiveness by:
    ●​ Encouraging or formally referring relevant findings (e.g., from the ongoing PUCT data
        center water usage survey or this rulemaking) to TCEQ for consideration in permitting
        processes.
    ●​ Exploring whether PUCT, as an interested agency, could support or join a petition to
        TCEQ (under 30 TAC Chapter 20) for rulemaking or guidance that prioritizes/streamlines
        approvals for non-PFAS immersion cooling technologies in large facilities. This would
        complement §25.194 by reducing indirect grid risks from water-constrained projects
        without expanding PUCT's direct regulatory scope.

Such coordination aligns with existing interagency practices (e.g., PUCT-TWDB/TCEQ data
sharing on water use) and would proactively address a key vulnerability affecting
interconnection reliability.

Conclusion
Adopting these modest expansions—disclosure and consideration of cooling resilience factors,
plus targeted interagency steps—would strengthen the final rule's ability to deter high-risk
speculative loads, minimize stranded costs, support sustainable business growth, and enhance
ERCOT reliability.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. I am available for any questions and urge the
Commission to incorporate these elements before adoption.




                                                                                                2/3
 Respectfully submitted,

                                    Digitally signed by Jason
